criterion_notes.c1: Examines drinking-water service provision and access via communal water kiosks in peri-urban low-income areas (LIAs) of Lilongwe, Malawi.
criterion_notes.c2: Satisfies both the plain wording and the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading. Under the plain wording, it examines institutional, legal, regulatory, and governance arrangements for urban water kiosks (Water Users Associations registered as legal cooperative entities, Lilongwe Water Board's Kiosk Management Unit, service contracts, WUA constitutions/policies, and state-backed traditional chiefs). Under the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading, it directly analyzes rule-type mechanisms governing service access: utility disconnection/rationing rules (<200 m3/month viability threshold and arrears enforcement), delegated regulatory/contractual ownership and management structure (formalized cooperative societies bound by service contracts with LWB's KMU), full cost-recovery and historical arrears-repayment tariff rules (coupled with elite honoraria policies that pass overhead and debt directly into retail kiosk tariffs), traditional chief discretion over land and governance, and bureaucratic utility procurement procedures delaying repairs.
criterion_notes.c3: Empirical qualitative/mixed-methods socio-legal case study drawing on primary fieldwork across two waves (Nov 2008–Feb 2009 and Nov 2013–Jan 2014), comprising 48 semi-structured interviews, focus group discussions, semi-structured questionnaires with 30 households, and institutional/tariff document analysis.
criterion_notes.c4: Reports concrete outcomes on affordability/retail water tariffs at kiosks (consumer price rising from MK 125/m3 to MK 300/m3, with the bulk-to-retail price ratio growing from 1:2.15 to 1:3.29), reversal of planned disconnection of 40% of kiosks (restoring water flow), and service availability/continuity (repairs taking up to 3 months, abandoned kiosks where repair costs were deemed unviable, shortages lasting 2–3 days, and supply limited to 2 days per week in some areas).
criterion_notes.c5: Identifies population and unit of analysis (low-income peri-urban communities/WUAs across 6 targeted areas in Lilongwe and kiosk-using households; n=48 interviews, FGDs, and n=30 household questionnaires), exposure (formalized WUA delegated management model, full cost-recovery and arrears-repayment tariff rules, utility procurement procedures, and elite capture/institutional bricolage), outcome (kiosk water tariffs/affordability, disconnection avoidance/kiosk abandonment, and service continuity), and study design (empirical qualitative/mixed-methods case study).
criterion_notes.c6: Published in English (with bilingual English/French abstract).

evidence_quotes.quote: In areas where consumption rates were below 200 m3/month and, as such, were considered ﬁnancially unviable, the Water Board planned to disconnect the kiosks. Implementing this measure would have meant closing 40 per cent of the operational kiosks. WaterAid Malawi’s intervention was targeted at reversing the rationing and kiosk disconnection policy.

The WUAs are responsible for providing services at the kiosk, collecting revenues from the consumers and paying the bill, including actual consumption and a portion of the arrears, to the Water Board (Area 50 Service contract, Article 7.3; see Figure 2: The WUA Model).

Fieldwork for developing the case study was undertaken from November 2008 to February 2009 and from November 2013 to January 2014. Forty-eight semi-structured interviews were held with representatives of WaterAid (both at the headquarters in London and at the ofﬁce of the Country Programme in Malawi), as well as WUAs representatives and key informants involved in or knowledgeable about the WUAs.
Opinions of local consumers were gathered through semi-structured questionnaires with 30 households in the area beneﬁting from the project.

In 2014, the ratio of the price of the bulk water (MK 91/m3) and the ﬁnal price to consumers (MK 300/m3) had grown from 1:2.15 to 1:3.29. The high price charged at the kiosks to consumers is the result of a number of factors. As the WUA has to follow the principles of cost-recovery and proﬁt-making, all costs associated with the incorporation of the local elite in the WUA and the repayment of arrears automatically translate into higher prices at the kiosks.

Last, despite the increase in price, the WUAs were hardly able to ensure improved service provision to their consumers: asset maintenance and continuity of the service remain of poor quality. In case of breakage, a response from the Lilongwe Water Board may take up to 3 months. The complex bureaucratic procedures adopted by the utility for the procurement of goods further slow down the simplest repair. Some kiosks have been abandoned because LBW considered the costs of repairing them too high and therefore not viable.

raw_response.exposure: Delegated urban kiosk governance and regulatory structure (Water Users Associations registered as legal cooperative entities under service contracts with Lilongwe Water Board's Kiosk Management Unit), full cost-recovery and historical arrears-repayment tariff rules, elite-capture overhead policies via institutional bricolage, and bureaucratic utility procurement procedures.
raw_response.outcome: Communal water kiosk affordability/retail tariffs (price rising from MK 125/m3 in 2008–2009 to MK 300/m3 in 2014; bulk-to-retail markup ratio rising from 1:2.15 to 1:3.29), reversal of planned disconnection of 40% of kiosks, and service availability/continuity (repair delays up to 3 months, abandoned kiosks, 2–3 day shortages, and supply restricted to 2 days per week in some areas).
raw_response.population_and_sample: Low-income peri-urban communities and Water Users Associations (6 targeted communities including Chinsapo, Mtandire/Mtsiliza, Kauma, Area 50, Mgona and Chimutu III) and kiosk consumer households in Lilongwe, Malawi; 48 semi-structured interviews, focus group discussions, and 30 household semi-structured questionnaires (units of analysis: WUA/community organization and consumer household).
raw_response.rationale: Empirical socio-legal case study in peri-urban Lilongwe, Malawi examining how delegated utility regulatory/contractual governance (formalized Water Users Associations under Kiosk Management Unit service contracts), full cost-recovery and arrears-repayment tariff rules, WUA internal honoraria/benefit policies captured by traditional elites, and bureaucratic utility procurement procedures affect household water kiosk affordability (retail tariff markups), disconnection/abandonment of kiosks, and continuity of water supply. Satisfies all inclusion criteria (c1–c6), including both plain and narrow rule-type readings of c2; eligible for systematic review mechanism synthesis as an empirical socio-legal study.
raw_response.study_design: Qualitative / mixed-methods empirical socio-legal case study (48 semi-structured interviews, focus group discussions, 30 household semi-structured questionnaires, and institutional/financial document analysis across 2008–2009 and 2013–2014).
